summaries.example: Imagine two students who each receive the same bicycle. One has safe bike paths and knows how to ride. The other lives where roads are dangerous and has not learned to cycle. They have the same thing, but they do not have the same real chance to travel. The capability approach asks about that real chance.
summaries.summary: The capability approach is a way of thinking about well-being and fairness. It says that people’s real opportunities to live in different ways are morally important. These opportunities are called capabilities. When an opportunity is actually achieved, it is called a functioning. The approach does not look only at money, goods, or official rights, because people may not be able to use them in the same way. A person’s body, skills, social rules, public policies, and physical surroundings can all help or block an opportunity. The approach is open-ended rather than one complete theory. It can be developed for different purposes, such as studying education, health, development, environmental questions, or justice. Philosophers also disagree about which capabilities should count, whether opportunities or achievements matter more, and who should choose or compare them.
key_ideas: A person’s well-being concerns what the person can really do and be, not only what the person owns.
Having the same resources does not always give people the same opportunities.
People are different, so fair thinking must notice differences in bodies, skills, social rules, and surroundings.
The approach is a flexible framework. Different thinkers can use it for education, health, development, and justice.
Capabilities describe choices that are available; functionings describe choices or conditions that have been achieved.
summaries.why_it_matters: This approach helps us notice unfairness that a simple count of money or possessions can miss. A person with a disability, for example, may need extra support to have the same chance to move around or take part. A right on paper may also be hard to use if transportation, safety, or social acceptance is missing. Thinking about capabilities encourages people and governments to ask what lives people are actually able to lead, while still respecting that people may choose different goals.

important_terms.definition: A real opportunity to do or be something, such as learn, move around, be healthy, or join activities. It is more than simply having a formal right.
A doing or being that has actually happened, such as being educated, eating enough, or traveling somewhere.
Conditions that help or hinder a person in turning a resource into a real opportunity. They may be personal, social, or environmental.
Something used to reach a goal, such as money, food, a bicycle, a school, or a public service.

questions_to_think_about: If two people receive the same resource, what else might affect how useful it is?
Should a fair school give every student the same help, or help each student reach important opportunities?
Is it better to measure what people actually do, what they could choose to do, or both?
Who should help decide which opportunities matter most?

summaries.example: Suppose two citizens have the same legal right to vote. One lives near an accessible polling place and can travel there safely. The other lives far away, lacks transportation, and faces social pressure or danger for trying to vote. Their formal rights are equal, but their substantive opportunities are not. A capability analysis would examine the personal, social, and environmental conditions that explain this difference.
summaries.summary: The capability approach is a normative framework for evaluating well-being, social arrangements, and possible social change. Its core idea is that the morally relevant question is not simply how many resources people possess or how much satisfaction they report, but what they are genuinely able to do and be. A capability is a real or substantive opportunity to achieve a functioning; a functioning is an achieved doing or being. The distinction preserves the importance of choice: two people may have the same capability while choosing different functionings. It also explains why formal rights and resources are insufficient measures. Conversion factors—personal, social, and environmental—shape whether resources become usable opportunities. The approach therefore takes human diversity seriously, including disability, unequal social power, and differing environments. It also distinguishes well-being freedom from agency freedom, since people may pursue causes or goals that do not improve their own welfare. The capability approach is intentionally underspecified. It can inform development ethics, public health, education, environmental ethics, and theories of justice, but each application must decide which dimensions matter, how they should be compared, and whether opportunities, achievements, or both should be assessed. The source also notes that the framework itself does not entail one distributive rule, such as equality or sufficiency, nor does it automatically amount to a complete theory of justice.
key_ideas: The approach makes two central normative claims: real freedom to achieve well-being matters, and well-being should be understood through capabilities and functionings.
Capabilities differ from formal rights because they require the conditions that make an opportunity genuinely usable.
Conversion factors explain why equal resources can produce unequal opportunities. They include personal traits, social institutions and norms, and the built or natural environment.
The framework shifts attention from resources as inputs to the beings and doings people can achieve, while still treating resources as important means.
Human diversity and agency are central. People have different needs and different goals, and the approach need not treat one chosen life as ideal for everyone.
The framework leaves major questions open: which capabilities to select, how to compare or aggregate them, whether to focus on capabilities or functionings, and how to assign responsibilities.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework broadens the information used in moral and policy evaluation. Equal income, goods, or legal rights can conceal unequal opportunities when people differ in needs, abilities, social treatment, or surroundings. It can therefore illuminate questions involving disability, poverty, education, health, gender, environmental conditions, and political participation. At the same time, its openness creates difficult theoretical tasks: deciding which capabilities deserve attention, how to compare dimensions without oversimplifying them, who has authority to choose, and how duties should be distributed. important_terms.definition: A person’s genuine opportunity to achieve a particular doing or being, given the relevant enabling and disabling conditions.
An achieved state or activity, such as being nourished, educated, mobile, or politically involved. It may result from choice or circumstance.
Personal, social, or environmental conditions that affect how resources and goods can be transformed into capabilities or functionings.
The distinction between what helps produce an outcome and the outcome itself. Resources and institutions are usually means; capabilities are central ends of evaluation.
Freedom understood as a substantial opportunity, not merely a legal permission or absence of direct interference.
The process of comparing people’s well-being or opportunities across individuals or groups for evaluation or policy purposes.
A broad normative framework that can support different, more specific theories and practical applications rather than a single finished theory.
The power to pursue goals, including goals that may not increase one’s own well-being. It highlights choice, participation, and different aims.

questions_to_think_about: Does justice require equal capabilities, minimum capability thresholds, equal functionings, or some combination?
When should policy respect a person’s choice not to realize an available capability?
Should a capability list be fixed by theorists, developed through public reasoning, or selected pragmatically for a particular application?
Can a framework centered on individuals adequately represent capabilities that depend on collective action and social relationships?
What additional principles are needed to turn the capability framework into a complete theory of justice?

summaries.example: Consider a school that gives every student the same laptop. One student has reliable internet, a quiet place to work, and accessible software. Another shares a crowded home, has weak internet, and cannot use the software comfortably because of a disability. The laptops are equal resources, but the students do not have equal capabilities to learn online. The difference comes from conversion factors: personal, social, and environmental conditions that change what a resource can do for someone.
summaries.summary: The capability approach is a philosophical framework for asking whether people have meaningful opportunities to live well. It treats capabilities as real freedoms: opportunities that are supported by the conditions needed to use them. Functionings are the capabilities people actually realize. This difference matters because two people may have the same opportunity but make different choices. The approach criticizes measures that look only at resources, public goods, or happiness. Resources are important, but they are means, not always the ends that should be compared. A person’s health, skills, disability, social position, local rules, public services, roads, safety, and environment can all affect how resources become opportunities. The framework also recognizes agency, meaning that people may choose goals beyond their own comfort or well-being. Capability scholars use the framework in development, health, education, disability, environmental ethics, and justice. However, it is not one fully specified theory. Different applications must decide which capabilities matter, how to weigh them, whether to use opportunities or achievements, and how much responsibility belongs to individuals, groups, or governments. Philosophers disagree about these choices, including whether a list should be proposed by theorists or shaped through public reasoning.
key_ideas: The approach asks what people are really able to do and be, rather than looking only at their possessions or reported happiness.
Capabilities are opportunities; functionings are achieved states or activities.
A legal right may be formal but not substantive if barriers such as distance, danger, discrimination, or lack of transport remain.
People with the same resources may have different opportunities because of personal, social, and environmental conversion factors.
The approach is used in many areas, but it does not by itself settle every question about justice or tell us one final list of valuable capabilities.
There is an ongoing debate about whether fairness should focus on opportunities, achievements, or a careful combination of both.
summaries.why_it_matters: The capability approach can expose unfairness hidden by equal treatment on paper. Giving everyone the same money, equipment, or right may not give everyone the same chance to learn, travel, participate, or stay healthy. It encourages decision-makers to examine barriers and supports in people’s actual surroundings. It also keeps personal choice in view: a person should not automatically be judged worse off merely because they choose not to use an opportunity. Because the framework is flexible, it can fit different problems, but that flexibility means that users must explain their values and methods rather than treating the approach as a complete answer.

important_terms.definition: A genuine opportunity to do or be something important, not merely permission or a right written in a rule.
An opportunity that has become an achieved activity or condition, such as completing schoolwork or being well-nourished.
A condition that affects how well a resource can be turned into an opportunity. It can come from a person, society, or the environment.
A resource or condition used to reach a result, such as income, a device, transportation, or a school.
The result that matters in an evaluation, such as being educated, healthy, mobile, or able to participate.
A framework that gives basic concepts but leaves room for different theories and uses.
A person’s ability to pursue goals and make choices, including goals that may not directly improve personal comfort or happiness.
A comparison of people’s well-being or opportunities with one another, often to judge whether policies are fair.

questions_to_think_about: Why might equal resources fail to create equal opportunities?
Should a school measure students’ final achievements, their chances to achieve, or both?
Who should decide which capabilities are important in a community?
Can people have a capability if using it depends on another person giving up the same opportunity?
What might a capability approach reveal that a happiness survey or income comparison would miss?
